newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end lower; bonds, dollar stronger.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end lower; bonds, dollar stronger.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks ended weaker Thursday after surprisingly downbeat economic news sparked a late sell-off of economically sensitive shares.
Bonds rose on strong demand at the Treasury's five-year note auction. The dollar climbed after a surprisingly large cut in Swiss interest rates hurt the Swiss franc and the German mark.
Heating oil prices closed lower after soaring on worries over low inventories in the United States and Europe as Western oil companies and consumers start preparing for the coming winter.
Blue-chip stocks ended modestly lower as an unexpectedly weak August durable goods report sparked selling in economically sensitive issues.

"The durables point to an economic slowdown and fortify the Fed's decision (on Tuesday) not to raise short-term rates," said Peter Cardillo of Westfalia Investments. "But a slowdown raises the question about future corporate earnings."

After early selling and a spate of late morning buying, the Dow Jones industrial average settled down 8.51 points at 5,868.85. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,388 to 999 on active volume of 499.8 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
A.C. Moore, senior investment strategist at Dunvegan Associates, said the Dow came under pressure "as the durable goods report showed there won't be the push in earnings for many industrial stocks."

The Commerce Department said orders for big-ticket items fell a surprisingly steep 3.1 percent -- the sharpest drop since April 1995. Separately, the Labour Department said weekly jobless claims jumped by 11,000 to 340,000 for the week ended Sept 21.
The technology laden Nasdaq Composite index rose 3.32 points to 1,227.98, but that was well off its 1,237.26 intraday high.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose more than half a point to yield 6.88 percent, down from 6.93 percent at Wednesday's close.
The dollar late Thursday rose to 1.2530 Swiss francs from 1.2415 late Wednesday and to 1.5230 German marks from 1.5170. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar rose to 110.63 from 110.47.
Heating oil rose to the highest levels in nearly five years before giving up the gains in late trading.
Heating oil for October delivery gained more than 1 cent to 72.80 cents a gallon after rising 2.08 cents on Wednesday. The price was the highest since early November 1991 after the Gulf War.
But profit-taking hit the market in late trading, and heating oil ended off 0.87 cent at 70.90 cents a gallon.

Heating oil has jumped more than 25 percent in the last three months on worries over tight supplies in the United States and Europe. The surge in prices has also helped boost prices of crude oil and gasoline.
November crude oil fell 30 cents to $24.16 a barrel, partly because of the late selling pressure in heating oil, and October gasoline fell 0.11 cent a gallon at 62.99 cents.
In other markets, gold prices slumped after news the International Monetary Fund may sell 5 million ounces of gold from its reserves to help the world's poorest nations.
October gold fell $1.70 to $380.70 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 ended down 2.5 points at 3,933.2. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average was up 110.70 points to end at 21,461.37.
